body:
Feser begins by heading off a natural assumption. Because he has defended Aquinas elsewhere, and because the book is called *Five Proofs*, readers might expect a treatment of Aquinas' famous **Five Ways**. A footnote lists them: from motion to an Unmoved Mover, from efficient causality to a first uncaused cause, from the contingency of the world to an absolutely necessary being, from degrees of perfection to a most perfect being, and from finality (things' directedness to ends) to a supreme intelligence. This book is not a study of those five arguments. There is overlap with Aquinas and with Feser's own earlier work, but the ground is different.

None of the five proofs is original to Feser — all of them are old, and he says so plainly. What is new is twofold. Several are arguments he has not previously defended at any length, and most of them have received little attention in contemporary philosophy. That neglect is striking, he says, for two reasons: these arguments were historically very prominent, and they are, in his judgment (he flags it as his opinion), the most powerful arguments for God's existence available.

His diagnosis is pointed. The neglect tells us nothing about the proofs themselves and a great deal about the state of contemporary academic philosophy, including the philosophy of religion. Readers of his earlier books, he adds, will not be surprised by this verdict. So although the arguments are ancient, they will be new to most readers, as will much of the defense he offers for them. The introduction thus opens with a quiet challenge: judge these arguments on their merits, not by how often they show up in today's journals.
plain: Feser starts by saying this isn't another book about Thomas Aquinas' famous five arguments for God. The arguments he defends are very old, but most professional philosophers today pay them little attention. He thinks that says more about today's philosophers than about the arguments, which he considers the strongest ones there are.
takeaway: The five proofs are ancient but neglected, and Feser insists their neglect reflects the state of academic philosophy, not any weakness in the arguments.
deepDive:
The hardest idea in this short section is also its most provocative: the claim that the neglect of these arguments tells us **nothing about the arguments** and **everything about the discipline**. Beginners are right to ask whether that is just a debater's move. Here is how to think it through.

Start with a principle nobody disputes: whether an argument is valid, and whether its premises are true, has nothing to do with how many people are currently discussing it. A proof in geometry does not become weaker because a generation of mathematicians is busy with other problems. Popularity is at most *indirect* evidence — it would matter only if we had reason to think the arguments had been carefully examined and found wanting.

Feser thinks we have reason to doubt exactly that. As chapter 7 shows at length, the most common criticisms target versions of the arguments nobody in the tradition defended. The classic example is the premise “everything has a cause,” which none of the five proofs uses. If the standard refutations miss their target, then the fact that these refutations are widely accepted is no evidence against the real arguments.

A thought experiment helps. Imagine a famous chess opening that fell out of fashion because a well-known book claimed to refute it, and suppose the book analyzed the wrong move order. Tournament players might avoid the opening for decades, yet its soundness would be untouched. Only going back to the board would settle the matter. That is what Feser invites the reader to do.

Notice the nuances. Feser does not say that every contemporary philosopher is ignorant. He qualifies his high estimate of the arguments as his own view (“or so I think”), and he openly admits the proofs are not original. His claim is narrower: neglect is not refutation.

This section feeds two steps of the module's argument. Step 2 appeals to the long tradition that held these arguments to be demonstrations. Step 6 adds that a demonstration doesn't fail just because many are unpersuaded.

The usual confusion is to think, “If these arguments were any good, philosophers would be talking about them.” The fashions of an academic field are a sociological fact. Whether an argument works is a logical one, and the book asks you to keep the two apart.

checks.q: According to Feser, what does the contemporary neglect of these proofs reveal?
options: Nothing about the proofs themselves and much about the state of academic philosophy
That the proofs have been decisively refuted
That the proofs are too technical for modern readers
That only Catholic philosophers find them interesting
checks.explanation: Feser separates the arguments' merits from their current popularity. Nothing in the introduction says they were refuted; chapter 7 argues the standard objections miss their target.

checks.q: Which statement best describes how the book relates to Aquinas' Five Ways?
options: It is a commentary on the Five Ways
It rejects the Five Ways as outdated
It overlaps with Aquinas but stakes out different ground, defending old arguments that are mostly neglected today
It defends exactly the Five Ways under new names
checks.explanation: The introduction says there is overlap but different ground: the proofs aren't original, several are new to Feser's defense, and most are neglected in contemporary philosophy.

body:
Feser defines **natural theology** as the study of what unaided human reason — reason apart from divine revelation — can know about three things: the existence of God, the nature of God, and God's relationship to the world. The word *unaided* is the key. Natural theology may not appeal to scripture, prophecy, or church teaching as premises. It must start from what any careful thinker can know. (The contrast is with knowledge that depends on God's having specially revealed something, a question the book sets aside.)

In his earlier books *The Last Superstition* and *Aquinas*, Feser approached these questions by expounding and defending Aquinas, whom he regards as the greatest natural theologian. That approach had real advantages, but also two limitations.

First, it was necessarily **exegetical**: it had to explain what Aquinas meant, or at most the directions in which his arguments could be taken (and were taken by later Thomists). That required laying out the background principles Aquinas relied on — about change, causality, contingency, and so on. It also required separating the essential philosophical ideas from the dated and sometimes mistaken scientific assumptions in which Aquinas occasionally expressed them. The result, in both earlier books, was roughly seventy pages of dense general metaphysics before the reader reached God at all.

Second, the approach confined the discussion to the arguments Aquinas himself happened to regard as most important, leaving out other significant arguments from the tradition.

The lesson for the reader is that natural theology needs metaphysics. You cannot evaluate an argument from change without some account of what change is. The question is only how to introduce that metaphysics, and this book will do it differently.
plain: Natural theology means figuring out what we can know about God by reasoning alone — no holy books, no appeals to faith. Feser's earlier books got there by explaining Aquinas, but that meant long detours: interpreting old texts, laying out background philosophy, and separating Aquinas' ideas from medieval science.
takeaway: Natural theology asks what reason alone, without revelation, can know about God's existence, nature, and relation to the world — and doing it through commentary on Aquinas proved slow and narrow.
deepDive:
The central idea here is the definition of natural theology, and it is worth slowing down on each part.

**“Unaided human reason.”** This does not mean reasoning without philosophy, or without experience. The Aristotelian proof starts from something we know by experience — that things change. What it excludes is appealing to authority or revelation as a premise. A useful test: could a thoughtful pagan, atheist, or agnostic in principle check this premise for himself? “Coffee cools when left on the desk” passes. “Scripture says God made the heavens” does not, because accepting it already presupposes that God has spoken.

**“Apart from divine revelation.”** Natural theology is not *opposed* to revelation. Feser's closing paragraphs make clear that revelation is simply a further question, which the book leaves open. Many traditions hold that some truths about God (that God exists and is all-powerful) can be known both by reason and by revelation, while others (such as the Trinity) are known by revelation alone.

**Three topics: existence, nature, relationship to the world.** These map onto the book's structure. Stage 1 of each proof addresses existence. Stage 2 and chapter 6 address God's nature. Chapter 6's treatment of conservation, concurrence, and miracles addresses God's relationship to the world.

Next, why did the earlier books need seventy pages of metaphysics? Because arguments like Aquinas' use concepts — actuality and potentiality, essence and existence, per se causal series — that most modern readers have never met. Without them, the arguments are almost guaranteed to be misread; for example, “first cause” gets read as “earliest cause.” The concepts had to be taught somewhere. The earlier books taught them up front, and this book teaches them on the spot.

This section secures **step 1** of the module's argument, which states the ground rules, and it prepares **step 18**, the limit of what natural theology can establish.

The usual confusion is to hear “natural theology” as “a theology of nature” — reading God into scientific findings — or as “naturalistic” theology. It is neither. It is philosophical argument about God from premises available to reason as such.

checks.q: Which of the following could serve as a premise in natural theology as Feser defines it?
options: Scripture teaches that God created the heavens
A church council declared that God is simple
A prophet reported a vision of God
Things in the world undergo change
checks.explanation: Natural theology uses premises available to unaided reason. The first three rely on revelation or authority; the fact of change is available to anyone.

checks.q: Why did Feser's earlier Aquinas-based books require about seventy pages of metaphysics before reaching God?
options: Because Aquinas' arguments are invalid without modern logic
Because explaining Aquinas required laying out his background principles and separating them from outdated science
Because the publishers required a long introduction
Because natural theology depends on revelation
checks.explanation: The exegetical approach had to set out principles about change, causality, and contingency and disentangle them from dated science before the arguments could be understood.

body:
Feser saw a twofold need. The first was a defense of important arguments for God that Aquinas does not discuss and that recent natural theology has under-examined. The second was a presentation of *all* the most important arguments that skips textual exegesis and long metaphysical preliminaries. It would get straight to the heart of each argument and introduce background principles only when they are needed.

That is what the book does. Two of the five proofs can be found in Aquinas; three are not arguments he discusses, at least not at length or in the form presented. The roadmap shows that the Aristotelian proof corresponds to Aquinas' First Way and that the Thomistic proof is the argument of his *On Being and Essence*. Aquinas also gave some expression to the Neo-Platonic idea.

There is no exegesis of Aquinas or anyone else. The proofs are inspired by five great thinkers:

- **Aristotle**, behind the Aristotelian proof (chapter 1)
- **Plotinus**, behind the Neo-Platonic proof (chapter 2)
- **Augustine**, behind the Augustinian proof (chapter 3)
- **Aquinas**, behind the Thomistic proof (chapter 4)
- **Leibniz**, behind the rationalist proof (chapter 5)

Feser thinks the proofs capture what is essential in those thinkers' reasoning. But he is not interpreting their texts or claiming they would agree with everything he says. It is an *Aristotelian* proof, not exactly Aristotle's own; an *Augustinian* proof, not a reading of anything Augustine wrote. And background metaphysics is kept to the minimum, introduced along the way as each argument requires it. This changes how the reader should evaluate the proofs: the question is never “Is this what Aristotle said?” but “Is this argument sound?”
plain: This book skips the history lessons. It takes five arguments inspired by great thinkers — Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Aquinas, and Leibniz — and defends each one on its own terms. Background ideas are explained only when an argument needs them.
takeaway: The book defends arguments in the spirit of great thinkers rather than interpreting their texts, so each proof must be judged on its own merits, not on historical fidelity.
deepDive:
The key distinction in this section is between **interpreting a thinker** and **defending an argument inspired by that thinker**. It sounds like a fine point, but it changes what counts as a relevant objection.

Consider an analogy. An architect today designs a “Roman arch” using modern steel-reinforced concrete. It is Roman in principle, because it uses the load-bearing geometry the Romans discovered. But it is not a reconstruction of any particular Roman bridge. If you want to know whether it will stand, you don't ask a historian what Vitruvius wrote; you check the engineering. Feser's proofs are like that. They are Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, Augustinian, Thomistic, and rationalist in principle, and their soundness is checked by philosophy, not by textual scholarship.

Two consequences follow.

First, objections of the form “Aristotle also believed in celestial spheres” or “Augustine never put it that way” are beside the point. Even if true, they don't touch the argument as stated.

Second, and less obviously, the method commits Feser to making each argument work by its own lights. He cannot lean on the authority of a great name. That is a harder standard, not an easier one.

Notice two qualifications. Feser does claim the proofs capture what is *essential* in these thinkers, so he is not borrowing names loosely. And later chapters still cite historical figures and later commentators where helpful. Avoiding exegesis doesn't mean avoiding history altogether.

The “along the way” method matters for how you read. Key concepts are introduced where they are first needed: actuality and potentiality, and hierarchical causal series, in chapter 1; composition in chapter 2; universals in chapter 3; the essence–existence distinction in chapter 4; the principle of sufficient reason in chapter 5. Later chapters build on earlier ones, so it pays to read in order.

This section underwrites **step 17** (the book's method) and the distinction between “inspired defense” and “exegesis.”

The usual confusion is to think that an argument “inspired by Aquinas” must be a Catholic or specifically Christian argument. The inspirations include a pagan (Aristotle), a pagan Neo-Platonist (Plotinus), and Leibniz, a Protestant. More importantly, the premises are philosophical and available to anyone.

checks.q: A critic says: “Augustine never argued in exactly this way, so the Augustinian proof is a fraud.” What is the best reply in light of this section?
options: Augustine actually did argue in exactly this way
The proof is an interpretation of Augustine's texts and so must be accurate
The book defends an argument inspired by Augustine, not an exegesis of his writings, so the question is whether the argument is sound
Historical accuracy is irrelevant because the proof relies on revelation
checks.explanation: Feser explicitly says his Augustinian proof is not an exegesis of Augustine. Its merit depends on its soundness. The last option is wrong because the proofs don't rely on revelation.

checks.q: How does this book handle the background metaphysics the arguments require?
options: It introduces the principles along the way, as each argument needs them
It presents about seventy pages of metaphysics first
It assumes the reader already knows Scholastic philosophy
It avoids metaphysics altogether
checks.explanation: Unlike the earlier books, this one keeps background metaphysics to the minimum and introduces it in the course of applying it.

terms: Real distinction between essence and existence

body:
Chapters 1–5 each defend one proof, and each follows the same pattern. It begins with an **informal statement** of the argument in **two stages**.

- **Stage 1** argues that something exists which fits a certain key description. For example: “an uncaused cause of the existence of things.” In the different chapters the description varies: a purely actual actualizer, an absolutely simple One, a divine intellect, something whose essence is existence, a necessary being.
- **Stage 2** argues that anything fitting that description must have key divine attributes: unity, eternity, immateriality, omnipotence, omniscience, perfect goodness, and so on.

Why two stages? Because showing that *something* is ultimate is not yet showing that it is *God*. A skeptic can grant a first cause and still ask why it should be one, eternal, or intelligent. Stage 2 is where the book answers that question inside each chapter, and chapter 6 answers it again systematically.

The presentation is “informal” in that it is discursive and unhurried. It does not use the numbered premise-and-conclusion format favored by analytic philosophers. Feser gives two reasons. He wants readers new to philosophy to be able to enter and follow the arguments. And he needs room to digress into more general metaphysical issues, to make clear what is really going on in the proofs and to forestall misunderstandings and irrelevant objections.

The discussion does become technical, but it introduces technicalities as gently as possible. He hopes to reach both academic philosophers and laypeople willing to ease into abstractions. His image: every chapter ends in the deepest part of the pool but starts in the shallowest part he can find. He admits that this is easier for some arguments than for others.
plain: Every proof comes in two parts. First Feser argues that there must be something of a certain kind — for example, something that causes things to exist without needing a cause itself. Then he argues that this something must have the features people have always attributed to God: one, eternal, all-powerful, all-knowing, and good. He explains all this conversationally first, starting with everyday examples.
takeaway: Stage 1 shows that something fitting a key description exists; Stage 2 shows that it must be God — and a proof isn't finished until both are done.
deepDive:
The most important idea here is why Stage 2 exists at all, and how it works. Let's watch it operate in chapter 1, where Feser gives a compact preview.

Stage 1 ends with a **purely actual actualizer**: something that actualizes potentials but has no potential of its own that needs actualizing. Stage 2 then reasons roughly like this:

1. **Immutable.** Change is the actualization of a potential. Something with no potential cannot change.
2. **Eternal.** Existing in time involves change, so an unchangeable being is outside time altogether.
3. **Immaterial.** Being material involves changeability and existing in time, so the cause is not material.
4. **Perfect and good.** A defect is a privation, a potential a thing's nature calls for but fails to realize. Pure actuality has no unrealized potential, so it has no defect.
5. **One.** Two things of a kind must differ in some feature one has and the other lacks. Nothing purely actual can lack anything, so there can't be two.
6. **Omnipotent.** Power is the ability to actualize potential, and this cause is the source of all actualizing power.

Intelligence takes more work. Feser has to introduce the principle of proportionate causality first.

Now a thought experiment. Suppose a skeptic accepts Stage 1 but says, “Fine — the purely actual actualizer is a quantum field.” Stage 2 gives you a test. A quantum field fluctuates and takes on different states, so it has potentials. Whatever has potentials isn't purely actual. So the skeptic's candidate fails the description Stage 1 established. Stage 2 is not decoration; it is what rules out impostors.

Note the qualifications. The Stage 2 derivations in each chapter are sketches, and Feser promises fuller treatment and replies to objections in chapter 6. The informal style is deliberate, not a sign of looseness. The digressions are there to block misreadings before they happen.

This section underwrites **step 15** (two stages) and **step 16**, which answers the objection that a first cause isn't God.

The usual confusion: many people think first-cause arguments stop at “something started things.” Popular critics like Dawkins say there is no reason to credit a first cause with omnipotence or omniscience. The book's architecture is built to meet exactly that complaint.

checks.q: A reader grants that there is an uncaused cause of the existence of things but asks why it must be only one. Which part of each proof chapter addresses this?
options: The formal statement
The objections section
Stage 1 of the informal statement
Stage 2 of the informal statement
checks.explanation: Stage 2 argues that whatever fits the Stage 1 description must have the divine attributes, including unity.

checks.q: Why does Feser present the arguments informally before giving them in step-by-step form?
options: Because the arguments can't be formalized
To ease newcomers in and to make room for metaphysical digressions that clarify the proofs and head off misunderstandings
Because informal arguments are more persuasive than valid ones
Because the informal version is meant for laypeople only
checks.explanation: These are exactly Feser's two stated reasons. The informal and formal statements are for all readers.

checks.q: In the chapter 1 preview of Stage 2, why must a purely actual cause be unchangeable?
options: Because change is the actualization of a potential, and a purely actual cause has no potential to be actualized
Because it existed before the universe
Because it is too powerful to be affected by anything
Because it is identical with the laws of physics
checks.explanation: Immutability follows directly from pure actuality: no potential means no possible change. It has nothing to do with temporal priority or brute strength.

body:
After the informal statement comes a **more formal statement**. Here the argument is laid out explicitly, step by step, with two aims: to make its logical structure as evident as possible, and to recapitulate crisply the line of thought the reader has already worked through slowly. In practice this means a numbered list in which each line is either a premise (a claim defended in the informal discussion) or an inference (a claim that follows from earlier lines), ending in a conclusion.

Feser stresses that these formal statements are **not meant to stand alone**. A reader who skips the informal discussion may misunderstand them, because the informal sections are where the significance of each key concept is carefully explained. Words like “actual,” “potential,” “first,” “composite,” and “essence” carry precise technical meanings in the formal steps. Without the preceding explanation, a reader will supply everyday meanings and misread the argument. What the formal statement adds is a clear view of how everything in the informal discussion ties together.

Each proof chapter then ends with a long section addressing **objections** that have been, or might be, raised against the argument. Feser notes that these sections sometimes contain the book's most technical material. In chapter 1, for example, they deal with issues like Newton's law of inertia and quantum mechanics. Objections specific to one argument are handled in its chapter. Objections to natural theology in general, and the most common popular objections, get further treatment in chapter 7.

The structure is a reading plan: learn the concepts, see the skeleton, then test it against criticism.
plain: After the relaxed explanation, Feser restates each argument as a numbered list of steps so you can see exactly how it fits together. He warns that the list only makes sense if you've read the explanation first. Each chapter then ends by answering objections, which is often the hardest part of the book.
takeaway: The formal statement is a map of the informal argument, not a substitute for it; evaluate it only after the informal discussion has fixed what its terms mean.
deepDive:
For someone new to philosophy, the formal statements can look intimidating. It helps to know how to read one.

A formal argument has three kinds of line. A **premise** is a claim put forward to be accepted on its own grounds; the informal discussion supplies those grounds. An **inference** is a claim that follows from earlier lines. The **conclusion** is the final inference. The key questions are then:

- Is the argument **valid**? That is, does each inference really follow from the lines it cites?
- Is it **sound**? That is, is it valid *and* are all its premises true?

If both answers are yes, the conclusion must be true. That is what makes a demonstration powerful, and why the module's **step 5** says the proofs must be judged by premises and logic, not by rival hypotheses.

Here is a simplified illustration in the spirit of chapter 1 (not Feser's actual wording):

1. Change occurs.
2. Change is the actualization of a potential.
3. A potential can be actualized only by something already actual.
4. So, whenever change occurs, something actual is actualizing a potential.

Lines 1–3 are premises. Line 4 is an inference from them.

Now the danger Feser warns about. Suppose a later line says the series of actualizers must have a “first” member. A reader who skipped the informal discussion will naturally hear “first” as “earliest in time.” They will then object, “But the universe may have no beginning!” The informal discussion explained that “first” means *having causal power in an underived way*, like the hand that moves the stick, not *coming earliest*. The objection attacks a misreading. This is why the formal statement cannot stand alone.

The objections sections repay patience. They are often the most technical, because that is where the arguments meet their strongest critics.

This section underwrites **step 17** (the method) and supports **step 5** (how to criticize a demonstration).

The usual confusion comes in two forms. Some readers treat the formal statement as the real argument and the informal discussion as fluff. Others treat the informal discussion as the argument and skip the formal statement as pedantry. Feser needs both: concepts first, then structure.

checks.q: Which statement about the formal statements is correct?
options: They replace the informal discussion and can be read on their own
They introduce new arguments not discussed informally
They make the logical structure clear and recapitulate the informal discussion, but are not meant to stand alone
They are included only for professional philosophers
checks.explanation: Feser says the formal statements show how everything ties together, but readers may misunderstand them without the informal explanations of the key concepts.

checks.q: A reader sees a formal step about a “first” member of a causal series and objects that the universe may have had no beginning. What went wrong?
options: The reader correctly found a flaw in the argument
The reader skipped the informal discussion, where “first” is explained as having underived causal power rather than being earliest in time
The reader confused Stage 1 with Stage 2
The reader ignored the objections section, which proves the universe had a beginning
checks.explanation: The formal statement relies on concepts fixed in the informal discussion. Feser's proofs do not claim the universe had a beginning.

terms: Hierarchical (per se) vs. linear (per accidens) causal series

body:
The Aristotelian proof starts from the fact that **real change** occurs: coffee cools, a leaf falls, a puddle grows. It analyzes change as the **actualization of potential**. The hot coffee is actually hot but potentially cold, and the cool air in the room actualizes that potential. It then argues that no potential could be actualized at all unless there is something that actualizes without itself being actualized: a **purely actual actualizer**, what Aristotle called the Unmoved Mover.

The introduction notes the argument's pedigree. Aristotle developed it in book 8 of his *Physics* and book 12 of his *Metaphysics*. Later Aristotelians such as Maimonides and Aquinas developed their own versions; the first of Aquinas' Five Ways is one. These older writers expressed the argument using archaic scientific ideas, such as the motion of heavenly spheres. But, Feser says, modern Aristotelians have shown that the argument's essential kernel does not depend on that outdated husk. Chapter 1 presents the core idea as an Aristotle, Maimonides, or Aquinas might develop it if writing today.

Chapter 1 itself (not the introduction) supplies the key tools the whole book relies on. It explains why change can't coherently be denied. It explains why a potential is not nothing, which was Aristotle's answer to Parmenides' argument that change is impossible. Most importantly, it distinguishes a **linear** series of causes stretching back in time from a **hierarchical** series operating here and now, such as a cup held up by a desk, held up by a floor. The argument concerns the hierarchical kind, and it applies to the very existence of things at each moment. That is why it concludes to a cause that sustains everything now, not merely one that started things long ago.
plain: Things change — coffee cools, leaves fall. Feser argues that every change is something's potential being made real by something else that is already real. This can't go on with everything borrowing its reality from something else. There has to be something that is fully real in itself, which Aristotle called the Unmoved Mover.
takeaway: From the undeniable fact of change, the Aristotelian proof argues to a purely actual actualizer that sustains things now — and its core doesn't depend on Aristotle's outdated astronomy.
deepDive:
The hardest idea here, and the one the whole book leans on, is **actuality and potentiality**. Let's build it slowly.

Take the coffee on your desk. It is actually hot. It is also potentially cold, in a way it is not potentially a gasoline engine or chicken soup. Its potentials are real features of what it is, not mere logical possibilities. When it cools, a potential becomes actual.

Why does this matter? The ancient philosopher Parmenides argued that change is impossible. For the coldness to come to be, it would have to come from nothing, since before the change there was no coldness, and nothing comes from nothing. Aristotle's reply: the coldness didn't come from nothing. It came from the coffee's *potential* for coldness, and a potential is not nothing.

Next, why must something already actual do the actualizing? Because a mere potential, being merely potential, can't do anything. Potential coldness can't make itself actual, or the coffee would be cold already. Only something actual — cool air, an ice cube — can do it. That is the **principle of causality**. Notice it says that what goes from potential to actual needs a cause, not that everything needs a cause.

Now the premise's security, which feeds **step 7**. Try to doubt that change occurs. You consider an argument, then its next step, then reach a conclusion. That sequence is itself a change. So the doubt refutes itself. We can reject particular apparent changes as illusions, but not change as such.

Finally, the key move: **hierarchical series**. The coffee exists right now only because its water exists, which exists only because certain atoms are bonded in a certain way, which depends on how their particles are arranged — all at this moment. Each level's existence is actualized by another level *now*. Such a series can't consist entirely of borrowed actuality. It must trace to something that actualizes without being actualized. That is **steps 9–10**.

The usual confusion is to picture the Unmoved Mover as the thing that pushed the first domino at the Big Bang. “Unmoved” doesn't mean “earliest.” It means having no potential that needs actualizing, and so being able to impart actuality without receiving it, at every moment.

checks.q: According to chapter 1, why can't anyone coherently deny that change occurs?
options: Because working through an argument that change is unreal is itself a series of changes in one's thoughts
Because physics has measured change
Because Aristotle proved it in his Physics
Because denying change contradicts scripture
checks.explanation: The very act of doubting change presupposes it. That is why the premise can't be overturned by any experience.

checks.q: How does the notion of potential answer Parmenides' argument that change is impossible?
options: It shows that change is an illusion after all
It shows that change happens only in the mind
It shows that time itself does not exist
It shows that change is not something coming from nothing, since a potential is a real feature of a thing, not nothing
checks.explanation: The coffee's potential for coldness is not nothing, so cooling is the actualization of a real potential, not a creation from nothing.

checks.q: In Feser's kernel-and-husk image, which of these is the husk?
options: The claim that change is the actualization of potential
The claim that potentials are actualized only by what is actual
The motion of heavenly spheres
The hierarchical series of causes
checks.explanation: The archaic astronomy in which Aristotle and the medievals expressed the argument is the discardable husk; the metaphysics of change is the kernel.

terms: Hierarchical (per se) vs. linear (per accidens) causal series

body:
The Neo-Platonic proof begins from the fact that the things we experience are **composite**: made up of parts in various ways. It argues that the ultimate cause of such things can only be something **absolutely simple**, or noncomposite, what Plotinus called **the One**. The core idea is found in Plotinus' *Enneads*, and Aquinas gave expression to it as well.

Chapter 2 develops the idea with everyday examples. A chair exists only as long as its legs, frame, and seat exist and are held together in the right way, by screws, friction, and the right temperature. Those parts exist only because their molecules and atoms are arranged in certain ways. The dependence is not merely a matter of the chair having been assembled in the past. Even a chair that had always existed would, at every moment, depend on its parts existing and being combined. The parts can be physical, or they can be metaphysical constituents, such as form and matter or essence and existence. Whatever is composite needs a cause of its composition. A hierarchical series of such causes must end in something with no parts at all, since a composite first member would need a cause of its own.

Feser then makes a striking remark in the introduction. **Divine simplicity** is absolutely central to the **classical theist** conception of God, yet it is strangely neglected by contemporary writers on natural theology — theists no less than atheists. One of the book's aims is to restore simplicity to its proper place. This matters because, as later chapters show, a God with parts would depend on whatever combines those parts, and so would not be ultimate at all.
plain: Everything around us is made of parts — chairs, bodies, even atoms — and a thing made of parts exists only as long as something keeps those parts together. Feser argues that this can't go on forever. Ultimately there must be something with no parts at all, which the ancient philosopher Plotinus called “the One.”
takeaway: Whatever has parts depends on something to hold its parts together, so the ultimate cause must be absolutely simple — the doctrine at the heart of classical theism.
deepDive:
The hardest idea here is why a composite thing needs a cause **even if it has always existed**. Our instinct is to think of dependence as historical: someone built the chair. Feser asks us to think of it as present-tense.

Try this thought experiment. Imagine a chair that has existed forever, never assembled by anyone. Does it still depend on anything? Yes. Right now it exists only if its legs, seat, and frame exist and are joined in the right way. If the screws vanished or the wood burst into flame, there would be no chair, however long it had existed. So a composite thing's existence at each moment presupposes that its parts exist and are combined at that moment.

Could the chair itself be what holds its parts together? No. The chair's existence *depends on* the parts being combined, so it can't also be what *brings about* that combination. That would be lifting itself by its own metaphysical bootstraps. The combining must come from outside. And if the combiner is itself composite, it needs its own combiner — a hierarchical series. Such a series must end in something with no parts, since anything with parts would need a cause and so couldn't be first.

Notice the generality. The parts need not be physical. Feser notes that if Aristotelians are right that physical things are composites of form and matter, or Thomists are right that things are composites of essence and existence, the same reasoning applies. That is why the One must have **no parts of any kind**.

Why is simplicity central to classical theism? Because a God with parts — wisdom distinct from power, say — would depend on whatever combines them. That combiner would be more ultimate than “God.” This drives **step 13**: the proofs support only a God with no composition, which is why they don't support a theistic personalist “god” (**step 12**).

The usual confusion is to hear “simple” as meaning easy, primitive, or small. Divine simplicity means *uncompounded*. Chapter 6 even argues that it makes God harder to comprehend. A second confusion is to think the Neo-Platonic proof is about complexity, like design arguments. As chapter 7 notes, a pebble or a drop of water serves as well as an eye.

checks.q: Why does a composite thing need a cause even if it has existed forever?
options: Because everything has a cause
Because at every moment its existence depends on its parts existing and being combined, which it cannot bring about itself
Because the universe began with the Big Bang
Because it is too complex to arise by chance
checks.explanation: The dependence is present-tense, not historical. The proof doesn't use “everything has a cause,” a beginning of the universe, or improbability.

checks.q: Which starting example would suit the Neo-Platonic proof as well as any other?
options: The human eye, because of its intricate design
The fine-tuning of physical constants
A pebble or a drop of water, since any composite thing will do
The origin of life on Earth
checks.explanation: The proof concerns composition as such, not complexity or improbability. That is one reason Feser says it is not a design argument.

terms: Hierarchical (per se) vs. linear (per accidens) causal series
Real distinction between essence and existence
